children: The dollar on Tuesday scaled a fresh 19-month peak against a basket of peers amid bets for more aggressive policy tightening by the US Federal Reserve following hot inflation data and hawkish central bank rhetoric.
The US currency extended a 10-month high versus its Australian counterpart as a global selloff in AI stocks weighed on market sentiment, hurting the risk-sensitive Aussie.
A sharper-than-expected acceleration in US consumer inflation last week triggered a run of five straight days of gains for the US dollar index

, which carried into a sixth day on Tuesday with it rising to 103.66, the highest since April 2, 2025, when President Donald Trump rolled out his tariffs. The index measures the dollar against six rivals, including the euro, sterling and the Japanese yen.

Traders now view a Fed interest-rate hike at the next meeting in December as a certainty, and they also lay around 4% odds on a supersized half-point increase, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. A day earlier, those bets on an oversized hike were at nearly 12%. A week earlier, there were 16% odds for no change to policy.
Meanwhile, the tech selloff continued in Asia on Tuesday, with Japan's Nikkei
and South Korea's KOSPI

both firmly lower. A key test for AI sentiment - which has been rocked by the sudden departure of Nvidia's CEO, a Democratic sweep in US midterm elections and worries about a debt-fuelled AI infrastructure expansion - comes with the release of Nvidia earnings later in the day.
The dollar has been supported by the AI boom as capital flowed into US markets.
"Continued AI-related capital inflows and expectations of faster Fed tightening should support the USD," said CBA economist and currency strategist Carol Kong.
"However, erratic US policymaking and a sharp correction in AI-related equities pose key downside risks to our bullish USD outlook."
In terms of the Fed outlook, US retail sales data later in the day could offer further clues.
The dollar edged to a fresh 18-month high of 0.84075 Swiss franc
and rose slightly to 159.49 yen
Japan's currency has been hemmed in around 160 per dollar, which traders view as a potential trigger level for another round of intervention to support it.
The euro
slipped to a new 19-month low of $1.0985. Sterling
fell to $1.3172.
The Aussie
dipped to $0.6725, the lowest since January.
